content.summary_of_the_paper: In this work, the authors present a novel learning paradigm called Shared Knowledge Lifelong Learning (SKILL). Their motivation is that multiple agents can learn different tasks in parallel. At the end of the training process, these agents share information so that every agent has complete information on all the tasks they have been trained to perform. Because of the knowledge transfer, each agent is able to solve any task. To achieve a proper knowledge transfer between tasks, the authors propose a method that employs a pre-trained backbone, a group of trained biases, and a classifier for each task. To select the appropriate task for new samples, the authors propose a Task Manager. This task manager can identify which task a new element belongs to at inference time, making it possible to use the biases and classifiers specific to each task.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
S:
- This novel paradigm could be very interesting for the community. Many people can benefit from learning parallel tasks and then combine their knowledge.
- Focusing on agent communication is essential. As the authors mention, what one agent learns can be relevant to others. Limiting communication between agents is indeed a relevant problem.
- The idea of using Task Manager, although not novel, is ingenious. This idea can be extended to other methods, so they can be used in the proposed framework.
    - For example, in the same way that "beneficial biases" are learned, the model can learn masks (SupSup or PiggyBack) or weights (HAT) and use the task manager to identify the task-id.
  
W:
- Although the new paradigm is interesting, things are getting mixed up. On the one hand, there is the paradigm of learning several tasks in parallel, but on the other hand, there is the idea of ​​lifelong learning. We may have different definitions, but the bottom line is that LL is continuous learning in a stream of tasks. Learning tasks in parallel and then mixing the knowledge is valid, but not in the context of LL.
    - Without much knowledge of Federated Learning, I think the proposal is closer to this than to LL.
- I do not think comparing training speed sequentially versus parallel is valid since one assumes sequential training in which tasks arrive sequentially.
    - It would be better if the ideas were divided more clearly. The framework and benchmark offer valuable contributions separately. However, multiple methods can be applied that may transfer and accumulate knowledge. It is essential to compare it with techniques appropriate to that contribution. It is not helpful to compare only with sequential techniques. 
- Be careful with these terms like "student" and "teacher." When using Teacher and Student, one assumes that there is learning involved (as when there is a student and a teacher in a classroom). Instead, in the proposed method, there is only a transfer of information without learning.
- From the figures, I got the impression that some results are incomplete.
- Despite gaining training speed, if we compare the amount of memory used, it is N times higher than any other method.
- Many references to related works are missing. Study of current works is lacking.
- Fig 4, 5, and 8 are not very well understood. I recommend decreasing the number of comparisons.
    - For example, in Fig4, it is only necessary to place the best selection of hyperparameters for each method.

Q:
- Can the framework be adapted so agents can learn more than one task sequentially? This could better mix the idea of LL with Federated Learning.
    - In the text, the authors mention T=N, but they do not say how it could be done in case this is not fulfilled.
- Did you test as a baseline a model where the backbone is completely frozen and only train the classifier? In a sequential scenario.
    - I ask because I do not see much difference when applying your method with and without BB
- What extra information does Fig 6 provide?
    - I could have added the information from different methods in Figure 6 and deleted Fig 5.

The method can be called: Shared Knowledge **In** Lifelong Learning (SKILL). If Lifelong Learning is added properly.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
There are may be novel and good ideas in this paper, but they are not presented properly. 
I think there are important conceptual problems that need to be worked on before contributions can be properly submitted.
content.summary_of_the_review:
There are interesting ideas, but unfortunately, they are not presented correctly. The comparisons made in the experiments have serious conceptual errors, which do not help verify the contributions presented by the authors.

My recommendation to the conference is that the paper be rejected.

My recommendation to authors is to focus on contributions independently. With this, they can identify the experiments that must be carried out to compare correctly with current methods under similar conditions.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The submission introduces a novel problem formulation for multi-agent lifelong learning, which they denote SKILL, in which knowledge is shared across a population of agents operating in distinct environments ("physical regions"). Knowledge is shared through a communication network in the form of parameters or inputs. The submission additionally proposes a challenging benchmark of 102 image classification tasks, each of them corresponding to some standard image classification problem. As a requirement of the SKILL formulation, all agents must be able to perform all tasks seen by the other agents in the network. Empirically, the method achieves high performance compared to a variety of existing lifelong learning approaches
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
########### Strengths ###########

- The lifelong learning community has been looking for a formalization of the problem of multi-agent lifelong learning, and this submission presents one such formalization
- The 102-task benchmark is a highly complex benchmark that would certainly challenge any existing lifelong learning approach due to the wide diversity across tasks
- Given the assumptions made in the paper, the approach attains high performance

########### Weaknesses ###########

- While the problem formulation itself is general enough as presented in the paper, its instantiation into an algorithm and evaluation departs completely from the sequential nature of the lifelong learning problem
- Despite this departure from the lifelong learning problem, the baselines against which the SKILL algorithm is compared are faced with a standard lifelong learning problem, leading to a seemingly unfair comparison
- The technical and empirical contributions (in particular, the SKILL algorithm and data set, as well as the evaluation) appear to be of limited novelty and significance
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is for the most part clear and easy to follow. Given the clarity of exposition, the results should be easy to reproduce, although the authors did not provide access to the source code or data set (nor did they mention whether they would be included in the future). Some additional comments regarding clarifications and corrections that might improve the quality of the manuscript are included at the end of this comment as additional feedback.

The topic of sharing knowledge across a population of lifelong learning agents is of great interest to many in the lifelong learning subcommunity, and the successful creation of approaches that achieve this kind of knowledge sharing would be impactful to the broader ICLR community.

That being said, I believe the submission is not ready for publication, and therefore recommend that it is not accepted for publication. Please find below a number of questions, suggestions, and comments, which form the basis for my recommendation.

**On the problem formulation**

The general problem formulation is sensible: N agents are presented with a sequence of T total tasks, and must learn to solve them separately. After learning the tasks, all N agents should be capable of solving all T tasks, and for that they will be allowed to share some knowledge across a communication network. However, the submission then focuses on the setting in which N=T, and therefore each agent is not itself a lifelong learner, but rather a standard single-task learner. Doesn't this reduce the problem to distributed multi-task learning (e.g., [1])? This removes perhaps the central challenge of lifelong learning research, which is to learn over a sequence of tasks. There are other challenges, of course, such as estimating which task is currently being addressed at evaluation time, which the authors handle with a clustering approach. 

In some sense, this is just a matter of semantics, and the authors could re-brand their paper as distributed MTL instead of shared lifelong learning. And in fact, given that the authors themselves claim that the main metric they're concerned with is wall-clock time, as improved by parallelization, this indeed seems more fitting. In this context, the proposed approach assumes that each agent has access to a (small) set of local parameters, trained individually by each agent on its corresponding task, and a large set of shared parameters pre-trained in an off-line phase. Doesn't this combination of pre-trained shared and trained local parameters sidestep the complexity of distributed learning? Is it generally possible to make these assumptions: that a very small set of parameters, arranged as biases to a neural net and heads of a classification network, can be trained locally and then shared over a communication network to reach all other agents? And what would happen if we slightly changed the assumptions and had each agent in charge of solving 2 taksks (T = 2N)? Or many tasks in sequence?

**On the technical and empirical novelty**

The primary ideas behind the approach are: freeze the pre-trained backbone, use per-agent (= per-task) biases in the neural networks, and use per-agent (= per-task) output classification heads. At inference time, use a GMM or Mahalanobis distance to detect which task the current input corresponds to. While these ideas serve to solve the problem as stated in the paper, they sidestep the main problems of both lifelong training and distributed training: there are no parameters that a subsequent tasks must update to improve their own performance, there are no parameters that must be trained to agree across different training agents... Moreover, these ideas have been studied in various form in the literature. In particular, EWC (one of the baselines in the paper) introduced the use of task-specific biases for lifelong learning several years ago, and similar ideas have been used multiple times since then; task-specific output heads are all but standard practice in the field. One thing to appreciate is that the solution does focus on the notion of sending very little information through the communication network. In the basic (GMM-based) version, each agent only sends one classification head and the GMM means/covarainces, which introduces little overhead. 

Regarding the proposed 102-task data set, it is difficult to tell from the content in the manuscript exactly how useful this data set might be. While it is likely indeed the most complex image classification data set out there, from the body of the paper all we know is that it combines multiple data sets together into a single one. There are no insights on what characteristics make this combination interesting or how the tasks were chosen. Plus, while this might be the largest such combination, the same idea of combining multiple data sets into one bigger data set for LL/MTL has been used in the past [2]. One thing that might help clarify this contribution is clarifying Fig. 3 further. Are we to assume that each circle is one task from the SKILL data set? And shouldn't difficulty be 100% _minus_ accuracy? Should we assume that the difficulty in the table is also the accuracy measured on ResNet-18? Is this accuracy measured over the ResNet trained on all tasks jointly or on each individual task? As it is, we are missing a lot of detail that might better explain the usefulness of the contributed data set. It might also be useful to include some of this text directly in the main body (and not just the figure caption)

**On the evaluation setting**

Given that the problem formulation and proposed method are closer to distributed MTL than lifelong learning, it seems that perhaps the set of baselines considered for comparison might not be entirely fair. All the competing approaches must deal with the problem of catastrophic forgetting, while the SKILL approach sidesteps it by training on each task separately. The one challenge that the SKILL method is facing is the detection of the correct task during evaluation, but this challenge also affects multiple of the lifelong learning baselines (on top of the forgetting problem). 

Why did the authors choose to allow the baselines to train the entirety of the backbone xception network? While this certainly gives the networks more flexibility, it quite likely increases the likelihood of forgetting substantially, since a lot more parameters must be updated sequentially. Couldn't the baselines instead use per-task biases and heads like the proposed approach? Since these ideas have been explored in the past (as pointed out earlier in this review), I would think that would be a more fair comparison.

Are the agents also sharing their local biases to all other agents? Or is each local agent using its own local bias? I would guess it's the former, but this was never explicitly stated, that I could find. If indeed the biases are shared, in the end all agents have full acces to all other agents' models, correct? During the exposition of the results, any mention of multi-agent learning was completely dropped. My understanding is that this is a consequence of the multi-agent setting becoming irrelevant after all models are shared.

In terms of the metrics used for evaluation:
- While indeed SKILL is much faster than the baselines, I wonder if this is truly due to parallelization, as the authors claim in Section 2. Wouldn't the role of parallelization be voided when measuring MACs instead of wall-clock time? In fact, I would imagine that the results wouldn't be affected if the authors ran their algorithm sequentially, one agent after the next, instead of in parallel. The difference with respect to other methods seems to come from the fact that the other algorithms are training a lot more parameters.
- Was the quadratic cost of comunication taken into account when computing SKILL's MACs?

**Placement with respect to the literature**

It would help the paper substantially to include a section discussing how the proposed work relates to existing ideas in the literature. This might include covering lifelong learning approaches, distributed multi-task learning approaches, and common benchmark data sets used to evaluate these two types of works. 



############## Additional feedback ##############

The following points are provided as feedback to hopefully help better shape the submitted manuscript, but did not impact my recommendation in a major way.

Intro
- Up to this point, I was convinced this was going to be a very strong paper. The motivation was good and the claimed contributions and results were solid. However, given the fact that the actually instantiated problem and method for it were not truly lifelong learning, it seems that the claims made up to this point might not be entirely substantiated.

Sec 2
- The communication network is a complete graph, meaning that the cost of transmitting information to other agents grows quadratically in the number of agents. Are there settings in which this might not be feasible (either because some agents are incapable of communicating directly with each other, or because there are just too many agnets), and how would that affect the proposed solutions? 
- The requirement that each agent can learn to solve all other agents' tasks seems to suggest a few things. For example, in RL (which was briefly mentioned), all agents would be required to have the same morphology (i.e., the same dynamics), which is a strong assumption for a population of embodied agents. It also seems to suggest that the _underlying_ (evaluation) task distribution is the same across all agents, even if they observe a different set of tasks during training. This seems a bit odd given the phrasing that each agent is in its own unique "physical region" -- why would we then deploy another agent in this agent's region? It would seem that instead what we want is for each agent to improve its performance on _its own_ region, while leveraging knowledge from the other agents' regions. I don't necessarily think this is "wrong", but I do think it warrants some discussion and motivation in the paper. The "birds in the sky and fish in the ocean" motivation doesn't seem to cut it for this same reason: why would these agents be swapped?
- If space permits, it would be relevant to add some text briefly describing Fig. 1 in the main body, to help the flow.
- "SKILL agents must avoid sharing local or specialized knowledge that may be misleading, in conflict with, or inappropriate to other agents": why is this so? If all agents are expected to solve all possible tasks, don't they all require the entirety of the other agents' knowledge?
- While the motivation for constraining the amount of sharing is perhaps trivial, it would be useful to explicitly state it (e.g., comms are expensive or sparse or time-consuming or ...)

Sec 3
- Why mention RL if it is not included in the paper? This mention should be removed. 

Sec 4
- The back-bone is pretrained on ImageNet. Do any of the data sets come from ImageNet? That would skew the evaluation results in all kinds of weird ways.
- Is the GMMC trained on input or embedding space at the output of the backbone?
- It seems that the "Implementation details" subsection shouldn't be necessary, as all the details in that subsection are stated earlier in the section, as far as I can tell (except for the mention of Pytorch and the GPUs, which could easily be a footnote or a part of the appendix, not necessarily a 13-line section)

Sec 5
- It's worth noting that the authors do provide oracle task IDs to methods that require it, which gives some unfair advantage to those baselines.
- What do the authors mean by "the representative" of each category? Simply one to explain as an example, but the rest are still compared against? This should be clarified.
- What changes over time for the SKILL method that causes the GMM to make more mistakes over time? Isn't the whole training parallelized, such that the GMMs are all trained and shared at the same time? Same happens for 10 tasks. This made the training process seem somewhat unclear to me


Appendices
- I recommend the authors to use the appendices in a slightly different way. In the current version, they seem to be used as additional sections of the paper. They might be better used as additional information to support or expand on the arguments/discussions of the main paper. Each appendix should be referenced in the main paper, indicating its use and how it relates to the arguments on the paper.

Typos/style/grammar/layout
- Sec 3: etc[.]
- Sec 3: classes/task --> classes per task
- Fig 2 caption: two parentheses in a row, "vis" and "Appen" are not words or common abbreviations
- Sec 4: please spell out BPN the first time it shows up; it's not a particularly well known acronym
- Sec 4 (above eq. 1): citation to EWC and PSP in parentheses
- All figures should be placed either at the top or bottom of the page

[1] Wang et al., "Distributed Multi-Task Learning". AISTATS 2016

[2] De Lange et al., "A continual learning survey: Defying forgetting in classification tasks". TPAMI 2021
content.summary_of_the_review: The submission proposes one formalization for the problem of multi-agent lifelong learning, where agents train individually on their own sequence of tasks and share information through a communication network to transmit their local knowledge to all other agents. In practice, the proposed method assumes that each agent in fact faces a single task, and that there is no set of shared parameters across agents that is updated during the training process, sidestepping both the forgetting and the distributed optimization challenges. The solution approach is a combination of existing ideas that have been used by a number of other methods. One of my main concerns is the choice of baselines for comparison, which are all dealing with the problem of sequential lifelong learning, unlike the proposed solution. Given the arguments exposed above, I recommend that this paper is not accepted for publication at this time, and encourage the authors to dive deeper into the more general formulation where $N \neq T$.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a new framework for learning multiple tasks concurrently. A multi-head architecture is used, with a shared frozen and pre-trained feature extractor, together with a task-specific output layers. For each task, additional parameters are introduced corresponding to additional biases which can be added to the feature extractor (the backbone) in order to allow it to adjust to different input distributions. By allocating separate sets of parameters for each task, the authors prevent forgetting by design. The authors assume that the task labels are not present at test time. To deduce the task label, they approximate the input distributions of different tasks and use the approximations  to deduce the task label. Finally, the paper introduces a new benchmark consisting of over 100 image classification tasks, which can be of interest.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
I liked the idea of having a new approach in which different sequences of tasks can be learned separately but then their knowledge be combined afterwards. However, at present, the only knowledge combination is about determining the label of the task (and aggregating all different heads + learned biases). This prevents catastrophic forgetting by design, however, I cannot see how knowledge transfer is being attained.

It appears to me that the main novelty of this paper are the two task mappers (used to deduce the task label). However, I did not find a discussion on this approaches' effectiveness compared to related work.

Regarding the EWC baseline, the authors have decided to allow the finetuning of the backbone model which introduces forgetting and severely degrades the performance. At the same time, their method keeps a separate set of parameters for each task and then shows that the resulting method outperforms EWC. I don't find this result surprising or interesting. Similarly, the backbone in the other baselines is also unfrozen and finetuned.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall, I'm unsure on how the whole approach is different from learning separate models for each task (apart from the task identifier bit). The methods used for combining task identification are not compared to others'.  Therefore, I am not convinced of the paper's novelty, nor its relevance to continual learning. 
I would be more than happy to increase my score after reading the discussion, in case I have misunderstood or missed some important information.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper first introduces a learning paradigm where many agents learn in a lifelong fashion in parallel, and share their knowledge with each other (so they all perform well on all tasks). They call this 'Shared Knowledge Lifelong Learning' (SKiLL). The paper then looks at a specific dataset, the SKILL-102 dataset, and an algorithm that can learn on this dataset. They show results on this large benchmark and compare with many lifelong learning baselines, showing speedup and better performance (such as better accuracy and less forgetting).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

S1. The setup of SKILL itself (Figure 1) is very interesting and relevant. It is a difficult problem due to its generality of different agents learning continually over time and communicating with each other.

S2. The experiments are on large scale compared to most previous works (in terms of number of classes and images), so it is interesting seeing an application at this scale.

** Weaknesses **

W1. The SKILL learning paradigm (Figure 1) is very similar to federated continual learning, as in other works (some references: (a) Continual Federated Learning Based on Knowledge Distillation, Ma et al., 2022; (b) Federated Continual Learning with Weighted Inter-client Transfer, Yoon et al., 2021). A key difference I think is that (from Figure 1), SKILL requires agents to communicate with each other without going through a central server as in federated learning. However, despite this difference, I do not think this SKILL learning paradigm needs a separate name: it is similar enough to previous paradigms / papers. 

W2. The SKILL learning paradigm in Figure 1 is very different to both the SKILL-102 benchmark as well as the algorithm implemented in the paper. It is so different that I do not view the actual results of the paper as related to Figure 1 at all. In fact, from what I understand, the way it is implemented is (almost) exactly federated learning. I would be very happy if the authors correct any mistake in my reasoning: 
- The algorithm/benchmark evaluated has only one task per agent. There is no 'lifelong' aspect in this. I don't think it's right to say you can do this 'without loss of generality' (as said in Section 2 third paragraph), as this affects the learning paradigm massively. 
- Federated learning does include solving multiple tasks and having agents that solve all tasks (I think the table in Figure 1 is wrong here: also, note that federated learning does do parallel learning). In federated learning, each agent has a subset of the classes from the full dataset, but overall you want to learn a classifier that performs well over all classes from the full dataset. Maybe one could argue this is subtly different to 'tasks' as usually defined in lifelong learning, but I think the difference is small. 
- It is federated learning with one communication round (at the end) only; often federated learning algorithms have many communication rounds.
- Because of the single communication round (or more precisely, the fact that all agents communicate with all other agents at all times), I believe the algorithms are identical whether or not there is a central server (which is what is usually assumed in federated learning). 
- Please see other papers for the links between continual learning and federated learning, such as "Partitioned Variational Inference", Bui et al., 2018. The two are very related, and this can lead to confusion over usage of words like 'task' and 'agent'/'client'. 

W3. It is not fair to compare the paper's SKILL algorithm with lifelong learning algorithms (that learn one task at a time). A key assumption in lifelong learning is that data arrives sequentially over time, whereas SKILL assumes all data is available at once (although spread in location/agents). This makes SKILL not a lifelong setting, and therefore it is not fair to compare with lifelong learning algorithms.
- Instead, the paper should compare with federated learning algorithms. Eg FedAvg and many others. 
- It is also not fair that SKILL has a pretrained backbone on similar images, whereas the baselines do not. This makes it much tougher for the baselines. Other ideas for interesting baselines might include (i) separate networks trained on the tasks separately with frozen backbone (although this does not solve all tasks so is not the same), (ii) a single network that trains its parameters (head parameters and any other parameters, eg BB parameters) on all data, as if it were available in one place / one agent. Presumably this would perform well, but might be slower to train. Note that one can use GPU parallelism to speed up training by using many GPUs (but there would be high communication cost). These are the kinds of baselines people also often use in federated learning. 

W4. Where did the alpha=1000 MACs/byte parameter come from? Why is this a reasonable trade-off value? To me, without any context, this value seems completely arbitrary. 

W5: The authors say that they have 'successfully applied SKILL to visually-guided RL' (Section 3), but this is not a helpful statement for me, as no further information is provided on the setup or results. 

W6: The Beneficial Biases used in this paper, that are task-specific, seem very similar to the task-specific FiLM layers in "Generalized Variational Continual Learning", Loo et al., 2021. I think the differences are that FiLM layers also have a multiplicative factor, and are after the activation functions, whereas BB are before the activation function. But the two are still highly related. 

W7: I do not understand how accuracy can ever increase in Figure 4 for the SKILL algorithm + GMMC (which does happen sometimes as you go along the x-axis), and therefore may be misunderstanding something. Presumably, as we move across the x-axis, another set of Gaussians are added (for GMMC), and accuracy may get worse as some images are not assigned to the correct task. But, presumably, as we move further along the x-axis, and more tasks and Gaussian are added, the previous Gaussians all remain the same, and therefore performance can strictly never increase (any image assigned to the wrong task will always continue to be assigned to the wrong task)? Instead, sometimes the lines in Figure 1 go up in accuracy.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Although the writing is of good quality, I found the authors often confused concepts to do with lifelong learning and federated learning, and this made the paper much harder to read. I also do not think the SKILL learning paradigm is particularly original.
content.summary_of_the_review: For the reasons listed in my weaknesses section, I recommend rejecting the paper. It is impressive to get the results the paper has on the task they present, but they claim things that are wrong, and compare with baselines that I do not think are fair.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
